clinicalPearls: Mannose-binding lectin is a pattern-recognition protein that initiates the lectin pathway of complement by binding carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces
Low MBL levels are common in the general population, arising from polymorphisms in the MBL2 gene, and many people with low levels are entirely healthy
MBL deficiency is therefore best regarded as a susceptibility factor or disease modifier rather than a strong stand-alone immunodeficiency
Any increased infection risk is generally modest and most apparent in infancy, when adaptive immunity is still developing, or when combined with another immune defect or immunosuppression
Reported associations include recurrent respiratory infections in young children and a greater burden of infection in patients undergoing chemotherapy or with other coexisting deficiencies
The organisms involved are typically pyogenic bacteria, reflecting impaired complement-mediated opsonisation
Diagnosis relies on measuring serum MBL levels and, where relevant, MBL2 genotyping, while interpreting results cautiously in the light of the high population prevalence of low levels

There is no specific replacement therapy in routine use; management is supportive, with attention to vaccination, prompt treatment of infections, and evaluation for additional or more significant immune defects
reference.pathophysiology: Mannose-binding lectin is a serum collectin that recognises repeating sugar patterns on the surface of many microorganisms. On binding, it activates associated serine proteases (MASPs) to trigger the lectin pathway of complement, promoting opsonisation and clearance of pathogens independently of antibody. Common MBL2 polymorphisms reduce circulating MBL levels or impair its function, modestly weakening this early, antibody-independent arm of innate defence. Because other complement pathways and adaptive immunity usually compensate, the clinical impact is limited in most individuals; susceptibility becomes more evident when MBL deficiency coexists with immaturity of the immune system, immunosuppression, or another immune defect.

redFlags: Recurrent or severe infection that is disproportionate to isolated MBL deficiency, prompting a search for an additional immune defect
Serious infection during chemotherapy or other immunosuppression where MBL deficiency may compound risk
Invasive pyogenic infection needing prompt treatment

reference.prognosis: The prognosis for isolated MBL deficiency is generally excellent, as most affected individuals have no significant clinical consequences; the main relevance is as a modifier that can worsen outcomes when combined with immune immaturity, immunosuppression, or another immunodeficiency.
pitfalls: Over-attributing recurrent infections to MBL deficiency and stopping the workup prematurely, missing a more important coexisting defect
Treating an incidental low MBL level in a healthy person as a clinically significant disease
Failing to interpret MBL levels against the high population prevalence of low values
Neglecting standard vaccination and infection-prevention measures
Assuming a specific replacement therapy exists when management is essentially supportive
management: No specific replacement therapy exists; care centres on prompt recognition and treatment of infection
Early empirical antibacterial therapy targeting pyogenic bacteria during intercurrent infections
Ensure full routine immunisation, including pneumococcal and other encapsulated-organism vaccines
Identify and mitigate coexisting immunosuppression or additional immune defects that unmask susceptibility
Heightened surveillance during infancy and periods of chemotherapy or immunosuppression
Investigate for a more significant coexisting immunodeficiency where infections are recurrent or severe
Patient education and reassurance given the generally benign course of isolated deficiency
